visual_text: What gets counted
Should carer support be judged by a later care home move?
Two trials of programmes for family carers of people with dementia
Alasdair MacLullich
Livingston et al., Br J Psychiatry, 2020; Mittelman et al., Neurology, 2006
What gets counted
Two trials, two different results
UK trial
UK: START, 260 carers, 8 coping sessions
Carers' anxiety and depression: lower over 6 years of follow-up (modest difference)
Time to care home move: no clear difference (wide range of results)
US trial
US: 406 spouse carers of people with Alzheimer disease, counselling and support
Time to nursing home move: later, model estimate of the difference in median time about 18 months (557 days)
Different people, eras and designs. Not a head-to-head comparison.
Alasdair MacLullich
Livingston et al., Br J Psychiatry, 2020; Mittelman et al., Neurology, 2006
What gets counted
Our judgement
We should judge carer support first by the carer's own health
A later care home move is not automatically a better outcome, and an earlier one is not automatically a failure.
Alasdair MacLullich

Two-column comparison. UK START trial, 260 carers, 8 coping sessions: carers' anxiety and depression lower over 6 years, a modest difference; no clear difference in time to care home move. US trial, 406 spouse carers: later nursing home move, about 18 months by model estimate. Not a head-to-head comparison.

Statement card marked as our judgement: we should judge carer support first by the carer's own health. A later care home move is not automatically a better outcome, and an earlier one is not automatically a failure.
